title: Certificates and PKI Ops
objective: By the end of this lesson you can run the certificate lifecycle, check revocation with CRL and OCSP, and diagnose the certificate errors a help desk actually sees.

blocks.text: A certificate is born from a certificate signing request (CSR): the applicant keeps the private key, the CA signs the public key plus identity into a certificate. The life of a certificate runs: request, validate identity, issue, deploy, monitor expiry, renew, and eventually revoke or expire. Automation tools renew certificates before expiry, because an expired certificate on a load balancer is a self-inflicted outage.

items: Root CA: the offline, ultra-protected trust anchor.
Intermediate CA: issues on the root's behalf, so the root stays offline.
Chain of trust: device verifies leaf up through intermediate to a trusted root.
Wildcard certificate: one certificate covers one level of subdomains (*.example.com).
SAN (subject alternative name): lists multiple hostnames in one certificate.
Self-signed: fine for labs, a warning sign in production browsers.
Key escrow: a protected copy of keys for recovery when holders leave.

blocks.text: Revocation is for compromise and misuse: the private key leaked, the certificate was mis-issued, or the site changed ownership. Expiry is a date problem; revocation is a trust problem. A CA may also revoke a certificate when the subscriber violates its terms.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Error-to-cause mapping is the tested skill: 'certificate expired' means date, 'untrusted root' means a missing or self-signed chain, 'hostname mismatch' means the URL name is absent from the certificate, and 'certificate revoked' means check OCSP or CRL status. Match the error text to the cause.

blocks.title: Diagnose three browser warnings
steps: Warnings: (1) NETERR cert not trusted on an internal app with a self-signed certificate; (2) hostname mismatch when visiting www subdomain of a site whose certificate lists only the apex domain; (3) certificate revoked on a partner portal.
Name the fix that keeps security intact, per case.
Decide which case is a life-cycle fix versus a trust fix.
blocks.expected: 1: self-signed chain; fix by issuing from an internal CA the devices trust. 2: SAN or wildcard covering the www name; reissue including all names. 3: revocation; the partner must replace the certificate, and your browser is right to block. Case 3 is a trust problem; cases 1 and 2 are issuance and configuration problems.

cheatsheet: Lifecycle: CSR, identity validation, issue, deploy, monitor expiry, renew, revoke or expire; automate renewal.
Chain of trust: leaf, intermediate, root; the root stays offline.
CRL = full list download; OCSP = per-certificate check; stapling = server supplies a signed fresh answer.
Revocation reasons: key compromise, mis-issuance, misuse. Expiry is a date problem, revocation a trust problem.
Wildcard covers one level of subdomains; SAN lists multiple names; production avoids self-signed.

checkpoint.prompt: Browsers reject a site whose private key was published in a public code repository. The key holder has a new key pair. What must happen before trust returns?

choices.A: Wait for the old certificate to expire naturally
choices.B: Ask users to click through the warning
choices.C: Restart the web server with the same certificate
choices.D: Revoke the old certificate and issue a new one for the new key

checkpoint.explanation: A leaked private key voids the certificate's trust, so the CA revokes it and a fresh certificate binds the new key. Expiry is too slow, and reusing the certificate or ignoring warnings leaves the compromise active.
